content: Gothic architecture was widely used in Britain between the 12th and 16th centuries, mainly for cathedrals and churches. It is recognised by pointed arches, ribbed vaults, flying buttresses, tall towers, and large stained-glass windows. These features allowed buildings to become taller while filling interiors with natural light. Famous examples include Westminster Abbey, York Minster, Salisbury Cathedral, Lincoln Cathedral, and Canterbury Cathedral. Gothic architecture is admired for its engineering, craftsmanship, and lasting influence on British heritage.

Georgian architecture became popular during the 18th and early 19th centuries. Inspired by classical Greek and Roman design, it emphasises symmetry, balance, and proportion. Common features include brick or stone walls, sash windows, central entrances, and simple rooflines. Well-known examples include the Royal Crescent in Bath, Bedford Square in London, and Edinburgh's New Town. Georgian buildings remain valued for their elegant appearance and contribution to Britain's historic cities.

Tudor Revival architecture became popular during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It was inspired by traditional Tudor buildings while using modern construction methods. Typical features include decorative half-timbering, steep roofs, tall chimneys, leaded windows, and decorative brickwork. The style was widely used for houses, schools, and public buildings. Today it remains one of Britain's most recognisable revival styles.

Edwardian architecture developed in the early 20th century after the Victorian era. It is known for brighter and more spacious designs with bay windows, porches, red brick walls, decorative timber, and large gardens. Many Edwardian homes were built in expanding suburbs and reflected changing lifestyles. Today the style is appreciated for its comfort, practicality, and attractive appearance.

Romanesque architecture was introduced to Britain after the Norman Conquest in 1066. It is recognised by rounded arches, thick stone walls, large columns, small windows, and sturdy towers. The style was commonly used for castles, churches, and cathedrals because of its strength and durability. Famous examples include Durham Cathedral, Norwich Cathedral, and the White Tower of the Tower of London.

Queen Anne architecture became popular during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It combines elements of earlier English and Dutch architecture with Victorian design. Common features include red brick walls, bay windows, decorative gables, tall chimneys, balconies, and asymmetrical layouts. The style was widely used for houses, schools, and public buildings and remains an important part of Britain's architectural heritage.
